title: Upper Tribunal Partly Suspends the FCA's Motor Finance Redress Scheme: What Lenders Must Still Do, Who Is Challenging It, and When Payments Could Start
summary: The Upper Tribunal suspended parts of the FCA's motor finance redress scheme on July 2, 2026 on terms agreed with four challengers, so lenders need not calculate or pay redress for now; a hearing is listed for December 2026 or February 2027 and payments could slip to 2028 or later if the scheme is overturned.
description:
The Upper Tribunal has paused parts of the Financial Conduct Authority's motor finance redress scheme, which was designed to compensate people who were treated unfairly over commission arrangements on car loans. The suspension, ordered on July 2, 2026, was made on terms that the FCA agreed with four firms that are challenging the scheme, and the regulator confirmed that firms must continue to comply with every rule that has not been suspended. It changes the timetable for compensation, though not the underlying question of whether the scheme will stand.

The scheme itself was set out in policy statement PS26-3 and launched in March 2026. It covers motor finance agreements made between 2007 and 2024, which is a wider period than some earlier descriptions suggested. The FCA estimated that the compensation portion would cost about 7.5 billion pounds, within a total cost to the industry of around 9.1 billion pounds when implementation costs are included, and that the average payment would be about 830 pounds. The regulator presented an industry-wide, free-to-use scheme as the most efficient route for consumers and as a way to give firms certainty.

Four challengers brought the case. They are Consumer Voice, represented by Courmacs Legal, and three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes-Benz Financial Services and Credit Agricole Auto Finance. The coverage noted that some of the largest lenders, including Lloyds, Barclays, Santander and Close Brothers, did not join the challenge. The grounds are those that the challengers have put before the tribunal, and the reports reviewed do not set out the full legal arguments, so it would be premature to say how strong they are.

The suspension is partial, and the details matter for firms. While it is in force, lenders do not need to calculate redress, pay it or contact consumers under the scheme. They still must gather data, and they must respond to complainants who are not owed money under the scheme, which means that complaint handling cannot simply stop. The reports mention a seven-week grace period, giving firms time to adjust their processes. Dealers and brokers have a role too: AM Online reported that the National Franchised Dealers Association's Sue Robinson said dealers must provide documents within one month, so the information chain from dealers to lenders continues to operate.

The timetable depends on the court. The tribunal listed the hearing for either December 14 to 18, 2026 or February 16 to 26, 2027. If the scheme is upheld, payments may begin in 2027. If it is overturned, the outcome could be a revised scheme, in which case redress might be delayed to 2028 or later, or the FCA could direct firms to deal with complaints individually, which would be slower and more expensive for consumers and firms alike. Those scenarios come from the legal commentary reviewed, and they are possibilities rather than predictions.

For consumers, the message is to avoid acting on rumours. Customers who think they were affected should not expect a payment soon, and they do not need to pay a claims management company to take part in a scheme that is free to use. Anyone who has already complained should keep their paperwork, since lenders must still respond to complainants. If a firm refuses to pay or ignores a complaint, the Financial Ombudsman Service remains the route for unresolved disputes.

For lenders, the suspension eases immediate operational pressure but not the need for preparation. Data collection continues, so systems for identifying agreements, commission arrangements and customer contact details must remain on track. Provisions in company accounts will also need to reflect uncertainty about the outcome, though the coverage does not give figures for individual lenders.

For the wider market, the case tests how far the FCA can design an industry-wide redress scheme and require firms to follow it. The result will influence not only motor finance but also the regulator's willingness to use similar schemes in other areas. What to watch next is the final hearing date, any further directions from the tribunal, further information that the FCA has said it would give to firms, and whether additional lenders seek to join the challenge or accept the scheme.

It is also useful to be clear about what the suspension does not do. It does not cancel the scheme, it does not decide whether the FCA's approach was lawful, and it does not remove the obligations that remain in force. It is a holding position agreed between the regulator and the challengers while the tribunal considers the case. The FCA said it would provide further information to firms as the position develops, which suggests that practical guidance may change between now and the hearing. Readers should therefore treat any statement about payment dates as conditional on the tribunal's decision and on how quickly firms can restart their calculations once the suspension ends.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority, MPA, Financial Reporter, A&O Shearman and AM Online (July 2026)
image_alt: Legal documents representing a financial redress scheme (illustrative)
key_points: The Upper Tribunal ordered a partial suspension of the scheme on terms the FCA agreed with four challengers: Consumer Voice (Courmacs Legal), Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes-Benz Financial Services and Credit Agricole Auto Finance.

The scheme, launched in March 2026 under PS26-3, covers agreements from 2007 to 2024 and carries a compensation cost of about 7.5 billion pounds within a total of roughly 9.1 billion, with an average payment of about 830 pounds.
During the suspension lenders need not calculate, pay or contact consumers, but must still gather data and respond to complainants who are not owed money; a seven-week grace period applies.
The hearing is listed for December 14 to 18, 2026 or February 16 to 26, 2027, and payments could begin in 2027 if the scheme is upheld.

If it is overturned, a revised scheme could delay redress to 2028 or later, or the FCA could direct firms to handle complaints individually; Lloyds, Barclays, Santander and Close Brothers did not join the challenge.
why_it_matters: Millions of car-finance customers are waiting for redress, and the suspension means the timing is now tied to a tribunal decision. Consumers should not expect payments until the challenge is resolved, while lenders must keep preparing data and complaint handling.

title: UAE Insurance Premiums Grew 15% in 2025 to Dh74.8 Billion and Another 15.1% in Early 2026, as Health Cover and Higher Investment Income Lift Profit to Dh4 Billion
summary: UAE insurers wrote Dh74.8 billion of gross premiums in 2025, up 14.9%, with health up 16.3% to Dh30 billion and profit rising to Dh4 billion from Dh2.6 billion, and the central bank's June 2026 review reported premiums growing about 15.1% in the first quarter of 2026 to roughly Dh27.5 billion.
description:
The United Arab Emirates insurance market has continued to grow at about 15% a year, according to central bank data published in the second half of 2026. Khaleej Times reported on August 25, 2026, drawing on the Central Bank of the UAE's annual statistical report, that insurers wrote Dh74.8 billion of gross written premiums in calendar 2025, up 14.9% from 2024. The central bank's Quarterly Economic Review of June 2026 then showed the pace continuing into early 2026: premiums grew about 15.1% year on year in the first quarter, and press reports put the quarterly total at roughly Dh27.5 billion.

By line of business, property and liability premiums were Dh36.4 billion in 2025, up 14.1%. Health premiums were Dh30 billion, up 16.3%, and life and fund accumulation premiums were Dh8.4 billion, up 12.1%. The article notes that business-line data combining national and foreign insurers list health at Dh36.42 billion, which does not match the Dh30 billion figure and is not explained. Motor and transportation accounted for about Dh10.08 billion and fire for Dh6.89 billion. The number of policies was 17.3 million, up from 17.2 million, while health policies rose 26.1%. Health growth reflects a policy change: mandatory basic health insurance for private-sector employees and domestic workers took effect across all the emirates on January 1, 2025, which the central bank said provided "a stronger foundation for health insurance coverage."

Claims paid were Dh46.2 billion, up 11%. Health claims rose 15.1% and property and liability claims 13.8%. Two lines stand out for faster growth: marine claims were up 34.7% and fire claims up 27.4%. The overall gross loss ratio improved to 65.1% from 68.9%, and the health loss ratio improved to 75.3% from 77.4%. A loss ratio is claims as a share of premiums, so a lower figure means more of each dirham of premium is left for expenses and profit.

Profit rose sharply. Insurers earned Dh4 billion in 2025, up from Dh2.6 billion in 2024, mainly because of higher net investment income. That qualifier is important: it means the improvement owes as much to returns on the insurers' portfolios as to underwriting. Invested assets were Dh96.4 billion, up 13.5% from Dh84.9 billion, equal to 58.4% of total assets. Securities and debt instruments made up Dh43.7 billion and cash and deposits Dh27 billion. The solvency capital requirement ratio was 199%, up from 196%.

The first-quarter 2026 review points the same way. According to the central bank's June 2026 Quarterly Economic Review, as summarised in press reports, premiums grew about 15.1% year on year, the number of policies increased about 9.5%, and technical provisions and total equity also grew. The ratio of own funds to the minimum capital requirement rose to roughly 516% from about 393% a year earlier. These ratios are not directly comparable with the 199% solvency capital requirement ratio reported for 2025, because the minimum capital requirement is a lower threshold than the solvency capital requirement; the figures come from different measures and reports.

The structure of the market is stable. The central bank counted 58 insurers in 2025: 22 national traditional insurers, 10 national takaful companies and 26 foreign branches. The number of licensed insurance-related professions rose to 515 from 495. Changes to licensing are now under way. The central bank's Insurance Company Licensing Regulation, Circular 4/2026, in force since August 14, 2026, allows foreign insurers to be licensed only as branches and gives weight to an applicant's business plan, so new entrants will face a different test from the one that applied when the market grew to its present size.

Some simple arithmetic from the published figures adds perspective, though it is a calculation and not a central bank statement. Health premiums of Dh30 billion are about 40% of the Dh74.8 billion total, and property and liability premiums of Dh36.4 billion are about 49%, so those two lines make up close to nine-tenths of the market, with life and fund accumulation a much smaller share. Profit of Dh4 billion is about 54% higher than the Dh2.6 billion of 2024, a much faster rise than the 14.9% growth in premiums, which is consistent with the central bank's explanation that investment income was the main driver. Invested assets grew by about Dh11.5 billion over the year, which gives the sector a larger base on which to earn that income. Readers should note the limits of the data. The annual figures cover calendar 2025 and the quarterly figures cover only the first three months of 2026, and the press reports summarise reports whose full tables should be consulted for exact definitions. The Khaleej Times article does not explain the reasons for the faster growth in marine and fire claims. Even so, the direction is clear: a market growing quickly, supported by compulsory health cover, with improving loss ratios and strong reported capital, but earning a substantial part of its profit from investments.
source_name: Khaleej Times (August 25, 2026) reporting the Central Bank of the UAE annual statistical report, and the central bank's Quarterly Economic Review (June 2026)
image_alt: Dubai skyline representing the UAE insurance and financial sector (illustrative)
key_points: UAE gross written premiums reached Dh74.8 billion in 2025, up 14.9% on 2024: property and liability Dh36.4 billion (up 14.1%), health Dh30 billion (up 16.3%) and life and fund accumulation Dh8.4 billion (up 12.1%).
Claims paid were Dh46.2 billion, up 11%, with marine claims up 34.7% and fire claims up 27.4%; the gross loss ratio improved to 65.1% from 68.9% and the health loss ratio to 75.3% from 77.4%.

Insurers' profit rose to Dh4 billion from Dh2.6 billion, mainly because of higher net investment income; invested assets were Dh96.4 billion, up 13.5%, and the solvency capital requirement ratio was 199% against 196%.

The central bank's June 2026 Quarterly Economic Review reported first-quarter 2026 premium growth of about 15.1%, to roughly Dh27.5 billion, with policies up about 9.5% and own funds at about 516% of the minimum capital requirement, up from about 393%.

The market had 58 insurers in 2025: 22 national traditional insurers, 10 national takaful companies and 26 foreign branches; mandatory basic health cover for private-sector employees and domestic workers took effect across the emirates on January 1, 2025.
why_it_matters: The UAE insurance market is growing at about 15% a year, driven by health cover that is now compulsory for private-sector workers and by property and liability business. Profit is rising, but the central bank's data show that much of the improvement came from investment income, not from underwriting alone, so insurers' earnings depend on markets as well as claims. Strong capital ratios suggest the sector can absorb shocks, yet marine and fire claims grew faster than premiums. The figures also come as a new licensing regulation, Circular 4/2026, raises the bar for entering the market.

title: Australia's Payday Super Rules Start on July 1, 2026, Giving Super Funds Three Business Days to Allocate Employer Contributions or Return Them
summary: APRA's readiness letter of March 25, 2026 says funds must receive and allocate employer contributions, or return them, within three business days from July 1, 2026; the ATO estimates unpaid super topped A$6 billion in the last financial year, and SuperStream 3.0 starts on the same date.
description:
Australia's superannuation system has had a new timing rule since the start of the 2026-27 financial year, and it asks funds to move employer money into members' accounts far more quickly. The reform, known as Payday Super, was set to begin on July 1, 2026, and the prudential regulator, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA), wrote to the funds' trustees about readiness on March 25, 2026. This article is based on that APRA letter. We have not seen reports on how the first months have gone, so we describe the rules as APRA set them out and cannot say how smoothly they have been applied. Amounts are in Australian dollars.

The legislation passed Parliament in November 2025 and starts on July 1, 2026, according to APRA, and the Payday Super Regulations were released in February 2026. The central requirement for funds is that, from July 1, registrable superannuation entity (RSE) licensees, the trustees of super funds, must receive and allocate employer contributions to members' accounts, or return them, 'within three business days of receipt'. APRA calls this a major acceleration over current timeframes. The idea behind Payday Super, at the other end of the chain, is that employers should pay super contributions closer to the time they pay wages, which the letter does not itself detail; the letter concentrates on the part of the process that funds control.

Why was it needed? APRA cites the Australian Taxation Office's estimate that unpaid super was over $6 billion in the last financial year. Unpaid super covers money that employers owe their staff as super guarantee contributions and have not paid or have paid late. If contributions are paid only every quarter, a missed payment can go unnoticed for months, and a fast, regular process makes it easier to spot. The ATO is the lead regulator for implementation and administers employers' super guarantee obligations, and APRA supports it on the responsibilities of fund trustees.

Who needs to act? APRA names employers, RSE licensees, and the administrators, gateways, digital service providers, clearing houses, registry providers and others that sit between employers and funds. This is a chain: an employer sends a payment and data through a clearing house or gateway to the fund, whose administrator matches it to the member and credits the account. Speeding up the end of the chain only works if every link can process data and money quickly. That is why the letter stresses coordination and asks licensees to work with counterparties and other participants in the system.

SuperStream 3.0 also starts on July 1, 2026. SuperStream is the standard for sending super contributions data electronically. The new version adds a Member Verification Request service, which confirms an employee's fund details before contributions are made, and approves the New Payments Platform, Australia's real-time payment system, as a payment method. APRA reports that the ATO was concerned that a material number of RSE licensees were not on track to deliver SuperStream 3.0, especially the Member Verification Request service. We do not know whether that has been resolved.

What does APRA expect? It expects contribution processing to be treated as a critical operation under CPS 230, its standard on operational risk management. A critical operation is one whose disruption would have a material impact on members, so a fund must set tolerances for how long it can be disrupted and have plans to restore it. APRA says licensees should revisit their implementation timelines where necessary and engage with counterparties. Significant breaches of Payday Super requirements must be notified to APRA. The ATO and APRA said they would engage directly with relevant licensees on readiness.

There is a transitional arrangement. APRA says it will not prioritise supervisory attention to the processing of certain contributions that lack SuperStream data, until Treasury's planned technical amendment to regulation 7.07G is finalised. In other words, where money arrives without the data needed to match it to a member, funds will not be pursued first for missing the three-day deadline while the regulation is being fixed. The letter does not say when the amendment will be finalised, and we have not checked whether it has been.

What does it mean for members? In principle, members should see contributions reach their accounts faster and any shortfall appear sooner. The practical advice is to check your account regularly, to look for each payment after payday, and to report missing payments to the ATO. For employers, the change means paying on a tighter schedule and making sure that the data sent to funds is correct. For funds, it means investing in systems and processes that can match and credit money in days. As the letter makes clear, funds that fail to keep pace risk both regulatory attention and member complaints. Readers can find APRA's letter on its website. This article is a summary of regulatory guidance and is not financial or legal advice.
image_alt: Office towers representing Australia's superannuation system (illustrative)
key_points: Payday Super legislation passed Parliament in November 2025 and starts on July 1, 2026; the Payday Super Regulations were released in February 2026.
From that date, super fund trustees (RSE licensees) must receive and allocate employer contributions to member accounts, or return them, within three business days of receipt.
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO), which leads implementation, estimates unpaid super was over A$6 billion in the last financial year.

SuperStream 3.0 also starts on July 1, 2026, adding a Member Verification Request service and approving the New Payments Platform as a payment method; the ATO was concerned some licensees were not on track to deliver it.
APRA expects contribution processing to be a critical operation under CPS 230, and significant breaches of the requirements must be notified to APRA.
why_it_matters: Super contributions that arrive late, or never, are the money workers depend on in retirement. A rule that moves them through the system within days is meant to make missing payments visible sooner, and it puts operational pressure on funds, employers and the services between them.

title: OSFI's 2026-27 Annual Risk Outlook: Real Estate Lending, Non-Bank Financial Institutions and Liquidity Lead the List, With Targeted Plans for Canada's Insurers
summary: OSFI's Annual Risk Outlook for 2026-27, released on April 14, 2026, names real estate secured lending, non-bank financial institution risk (reintroduced) and liquidity and funding risk as its priorities, and sets targeted plans for insurers covering private credit, cyber, AI in underwriting, claims inflation and catastrophe resilience.
description:
Canada's federal financial regulator has set out what it will be watching over the year ahead, and the list includes both banks and insurers. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions released its Annual Risk Outlook for the 2026-27 fiscal year on April 14, 2026; Wealth Professional covered it the next day and Insurance Business on April 16. The outlook names three prioritised risks: real estate secured lending, non-bank financial institution risk, and liquidity and funding risk. OSFI's news release headlined that it had "reintroduced" non-bank financial institution risk, which means that item returned to the list after a period when it was not a stated priority. The Superintendent, Peter Routledge, said: "Canadians can be confident that OSFI acts early, transparently, and decisively to strengthen financial system resilience."

The non-bank risk is the main new theme. According to Wealth Professional, OSFI says that Canadian institutions' exposure to private capital firms and their portfolio companies has grown considerably in recent years and is now a material share of their balance sheets. Federally regulated institutions lend to these firms, to their portfolio companies and to their clients. OSFI warns that the opacity of the market "can mask structural weaknesses," that highly leveraged private capital firms could magnify losses in a stress, and that hedge funds, which use repo funding and derivatives, could unwind positions quickly if funding costs rise or margin calls arrive suddenly, with effects on markets including sovereign bond markets. Banks are also increasingly using non-bank institutions to provide credit protection on their loan portfolios through synthetic risk transfers; in a stress those institutions may have less capacity to provide protection, which could reduce lending to core clients, raise credit risk and weaken capital. OSFI's response includes supervisory reviews of exposures, risk rating approaches and governance, a loan-level wholesale data call covering non-bank and other corporate and commercial exposures, and reviews of counterparty credit risk management, stress testing and liquidity and funding provided to these institutions. It also plans a principles-based Credit Risk Management Guideline aligned with Financial Stability Board and Basel Committee practices, with feedback on its initial consultation document due on July 29, 2026.

On real estate secured lending and liquidity, OSFI's release says that housing and mortgage pressures have grown in some parts of the country, and that global uncertainty could affect confidence in funding markets. Funding cost and availability have stayed stable, but the speed at which a liquidity event could unfold remains a key concern. The regulator also says it is recalibrating capital requirements, so that some risk weights may rise and others fall over time, which it describes as routine maintenance. Revisions to liquidity adequacy requirements for specific retail deposit categories took effect on May 1, 2026, and a consultation on further liquidity updates launched on May 21 with the second quarterly release.

The insurer-specific plans, reported by Insurance Business, are detailed. For certain life insurers, OSFI will assess policyholder behaviour risk, asset-liability management and liquidity, noting that lapses and surrenders have become more volatile but remain modest relative to total available capital. For selected property and casualty insurers, it will do thematic monitoring of cyber insurance underwriting and the use of AI in underwriting, and it is watching claims inflation, especially in auto, and a softening commercial lines market. Selected insurers will face targeted reviews of their own risk and solvency assessments, including follow-up on prior recommendations, and cyber and technology risk reviews. Larger companies will undergo intelligence-led cyber resilience testing, and all insurers will face scrutiny of cyber incident response and preparedness. OSFI will monitor mortgage insurers for the effect of the housing market and will monitor catastrophe risk resilience across the industry. For boards, it will look at oversight of risk appetite frameworks, governance of complex technology and business transformations, and the independence and stature of combined oversight functions.

On investments, OSFI says it will examine insurers' private market holdings closely for effects on earnings, capital and risk oversight, and describes those assets as bringing increased opacity, complexity and potential illiquidity. Continued market volatility also creates reinvestment and valuation risk across asset classes. The article also lists geopolitical uncertainty, AI integration and execution risk from inorganic growth as other concerns. More than 1,100 transactions are reviewed and approved each year under the vested asset and DA-21 regimes, and the article mentions related-party reinsurance under DA-21 without a specific supervisory plan.

OSFI says the outlook is normally released each spring, and that an update may be published in fall 2026 if risks change significantly. It does not give risk ratings or severity levels in the release. In July 2026 OSFI also issued a separate regulatory notice recognising natural catastrophe bonds for capital purposes for property and casualty insurers, an example of how the supervisory agenda affects insurers' capital planning.

The outlook is a guide, not a rulebook. Institutions should read OSFI's full document for the supervisory approach, since the news coverage summarises it.
source_name: OSFI news release (April 14, 2026), Insurance Business Canada (April 16, 2026) and Wealth Professional (April 15, 2026)
image_alt: House keys representing mortgage and residential lending risk (illustrative)
key_points: OSFI released its 2026-27 Annual Risk Outlook on April 14, 2026, naming three prioritised risks: real estate secured lending, non-bank financial institution (NBFI) risk, which is reintroduced, and liquidity and funding risk.

On NBFIs, OSFI says exposure to private capital firms and their portfolio companies has grown considerably and that opacity 'can mask structural weaknesses'; it plans supervisory reviews, a loan-level wholesale data call and a principles-based Credit Risk Management Guideline, with feedback due July 29, 2026.

For insurers, OSFI plans to examine private market holdings for effects on earnings, capital and risk oversight, review certain life insurers' policyholder behaviour, asset-liability management and liquidity, and look at cyber underwriting and AI use at selected property and casualty insurers.

The outlook flags claims inflation, especially in auto, and a softening commercial market, plans intelligence-led cyber resilience testing for larger companies and industry-wide monitoring of catastrophe resilience; more than 1,100 vested asset and DA-21 transactions are reviewed annually.

Revisions to liquidity adequacy requirements for specific retail deposit categories took effect on May 1, 2026, a consultation on further liquidity updates launched on May 21, and OSFI says an update to the outlook may follow in fall 2026 if risks change significantly.
why_it_matters: OSFI regulates Canada's federally regulated banks and insurers, so its annual list of priorities signals where examiners will look and what institutions should be ready to explain. For banks, the focus is on lending secured by property, loans to non-bank lenders and funds, and the ability to fund themselves in a stress. For insurers, the items most likely to matter are private credit, cyber, AI use in underwriting and the effect of rising claims costs on pricing. For consumers, the outlook does not change rules directly, but it signals supervisory attention on mortgage lending and on the resilience of insurers to disasters and cyber events.
